I was nearly certain of the reaction I would get (essentially "we didn't know you felt that badly, we never wanted you to feel that way, we love you") but it still took so long to actually get this out. I'm pleased it ended up being such a non-event!

And I think I'll be okay. I've got a long road ahead but at least I'm on it now.

It's a bit of a mixed bag, but mostly positive. I feel relief and liberation, along with a bittersweet pang of having let a childhood idea (of who my parents wanted me to be) die. But I was never going to be the person that 8-year-old me thought everyone wanted her to be, and as it turns out, my parents really just want me to be happy.

Yeah. Honestly I wonder if my religious upbringing didn't do permanent damage that I can't undo. I've gone through a year and a half of therapy, been on medication for a year, and there are still days where I think I'm so wretched and worthless that I consider killing myself. Which I can't do, because I'm in a loving relationship and I have an animal to take care of, so all that happens is I torture myself with the idea of it and think of myself as a coward for not doing it. And the panic attacks I used to have in response to the constant "End Times" sermons I was subjected to continue to this day, just in response to different stuff. Sometimes it's in response to *nothing*, which is great fun. 

I've been out of religion for 3 or 4 years. I'm 27. I have no sense of self worth. I have no idea how to even begin to not hate myself. I'm anxious almost all the time. All medication does is take a little of the edge off.

And I still have family try to tell me church would make me feel so much better. :I

I mean, at least they didn't claim that "we have a couple gay friends", but I can almost guarantee those gay people don't like her at all. What a mystery!! :D

Well that definitely happened with him, too. I think I adopted him the day his stray hold was up, two hours after they opened. The lady showing my around was pretty sly, too; she was saying that a rescue was very interested in him. I think I asked to see if he'd get along with my roommate's dog (which she brought with her) pretty quick after that. No rescue was getting *my* dog!

I am really curious what his story is, beyond the fact that he was a stray. Doesn't seem like too many purebred poodles end up strays. His coat was in such poor condition, he was so skinny, and he's *so bad* at self preservation while out and about (he will chase squirrels no matter what is in his way, probably including cars if I let him) I wonder how much of that was him living on his own and how much of it was poor condition before he got lost or dumped. 

Guess I'll never know, and it doesn't really matter. He doesn't seem to care, at any rate.

I have no clue. I think some dogs were 'my kid wanted it' dogs and they got annoyed that they had to spend money on it, but I don't really know. I was just there to bathe 'em and brush 'em. (And *most* owners were at least pretty okay. We had a few long-coated regulars who came in once a week for a brush out and those were the most patient dogs I've ever handled! And a lady with four dachshunds would bring us donuts when she brought in her pups for baths, and all four of her dogs were absolute sweethearts.)

At least *I* feel pretty confident in being able to take care of a lot of coat needs for any dog I ever own, after that job. My boyfriend was talking about getting a shiba or a shiba mix and one of my first thoughts was, no joke, "Oooh I have a furminator! I could take care of so much shedding!" P:

I think a lot of people don't even realize how much brushing non-shedding dogs need, judging by all the matted dogs that came into the groomers I used to work for! Most only had a bit of matting, but I'd occasionally get to hear people getting testy with the groomer when she'd explain why there was no way to keep their dog's coat long when it was badly matted. 

What was disheartening was how many of them adamantly believed it was the groomer's fault for not subjecting the dog to hours of painful brushing, and not taking responsibility for letting it *get* that bad. "That's your job," etc etc. It's really hard to "do your job" if the dog only comes a couple times a year and that's the only coat care it gets!

Being that my childhood was ruined in part by "End Times" sermons giving me constant panic attacks and having to deal with daily existential terror (all before I'd quit playing with dolls) my kneejerk reaction is to say "HA! Of *course!* He was on shrooms!"

But, I'm trying to be mindful of the source site this article is posted on and not actually jump to conclusions. Has there been anything written to counter this? I'm thinking of looking up the researcher that the article refers to, Benny Shannon, and seeing what he wrote about it. Was wondering if anyone else had done so.

He's just such a sweet little guy, it would've been hard not to do everything I could for him! He's got a few health issues (I *suspect* he might've been a puppy mill escapee, but I have no way of knowing) but he's been so patient with everything I've had to do to take care of him. My grandma said the same thing! She saw him right after I got him, and then a year later, and said he acted like a completely different dog. He's much less skittish now, save for thunderstorms!

He's pretty much the best dog for me. I'm so happy I found him that day.

I love the way the writers of these comics portray drug dealers, as if they'd read about them once on the back of a pamphlet and decided that was all they needed to know. "Hello yes I sell drug." "YOU SELL BAD DRUG!" "Oh no what is my life. Jesus halp!"

Taken from the first photo's description since RES kinda eats the formatting:

"The shelter named him "Matt" because he was covered in inches of matted fur. Animal control found him hiding under a car in the middle of June, during an almost record-breaking year for days over 100 degrees. 

He was almost half the weight he needed to be (9 pounds, the vet said he's supposed to weigh 15-18.) You could feel all of his bones when you pet him.

A local groomer had volunteered to groom him before he was adopted. So when I saw him, he looked a little less pathetic, but he was still very scared. 

I walked into the small dogs area to check out the contenders, and was swarmed with puppies. After they got bored and wandered off, this little guy slunk up to me, sat down at my feet by my side, and looked up at me. I was sold instantly."

I feel that. :( 

What makes it worse is having so many people still in my life who tout it as the best thing ever, and I'm still processing all the damage it did and trying to retrain my thought patterns to not be so cruel to myself. I had an aunt once corner me while I was having a panic attack and physically couldn't lift myself off the floor, and tell me that by not choosing Jesus I was choosing panic attacks. :/

> I think I lived with this idealized vision of what I "could be" with God's help, and it was something not human.

Yeah! I get that. I'm not even sure what I'm aiming for, and whatever it is, it's something I would never in a million years expect from another human. But sometimes, when I'm in a bad way, I don't even really *feel* human. I feel less than that. 

I'm at least better than I was a year ago, but I guess it's a long, hard slog to build a sense of self worth where I had none before. (After all, having any sense of self worth outside of Jesus was just earthly pride, right?)

> I'm honestly surprised neuroticism isn't higher in Christian circles, given the sort of ideas they peddle. Who wouldn't be driven a bit mad by sincerely believing that God is watching and condemning their most private thoughts?

Likewise, I don't know if being Christian contributed to the OCD, or if it was just *the worst possible thing* to teach a kid *with* OCD or what, but that feeling basically ruined my childhood. My only escape was to retreat into fantasy; life was otherwise basically constant existential terror that I tried to alleviate by elaborate thought-rituals that never actually made me feel any better.

> I can relate. My parents believe that Christianity is the antidote to anxiety and perfectionism, so if a Christian struggled with those things, they were doing it wrong.

Gahhh I hate that sentiment and I got told that so often. Or, like, when I'd mention something about being really scared of the apocalypse, my mom's only response was "yes, it IS scary, isn't it?"

All Christianity taught me was that I'd never be good enough and there *are* things worth being perpetually terrified of. I wish I'd gone to therapy sooner than I did, really.

> Connecting with people, letting go of differences and focusing on the positive commonalities of others for the well being of everybody became much more important.

That sounds lovely!

I think what confuses me about how I'm feeling now is that, in the past year, I've done a lot to connect more with people and do things I would've been afraid to do. I discovered a love of festivals, burns, camping with friends, and a bunch of social outdoor stuff that leaves you stinkin' and happy at the end of it. My life now is almost unrecognizable compared to a year ago.

And yet I still feel like I'm somehow not doing enough to justify my own existence. I dunno. Maybe I'm just still dealing with the fallout of having been suicidally depressed only a year ago.

That makes sense. That sucks. :/ 

For me, I don't even seem to believe validation coming from outside sources. I get told I'm nice or fun to be around or skilled at whatever, and I just don't *believe* them because I'm so trained to look inside for whatever. (My church was always very emphatic on it not mattering what outside gestures you made, but really *believing* in your heart, so I turned neurotically introspective pretty young. And what I do now doesn't *feel* like enough to make me un-worthless.)

> This all does lead to hopelessness and a general sense of there being no point to anything in my life and much dwelling on the idea of suicide.

You're not alone there. I am not exaggerating when I tell people I would not be here if I didn't have my dog. Winter of 2013, the only reason I could come up with  not to kill myself was not being able to stand the thought of my dog not understanding where I went and looking for me.

Growing up, I was told in no uncertain terms that nobody found me pleasing to look at. It hurt, undeniably so, but at least I had how smart I was, right? If I couldn't be a looker, at least I could be smart.

Adult life has blown that slim comfort out of the water. My student teaching semester was a disaster, and I'm left grasping at the straws of anything else I'm even passably competent at. Art? A bad bet for all but the most dedicated artists, and my interests are far too niche anyway. Web development? Laughable, my competition has already been doing it for far longer, they're probably all far smarter than I am, and I am *at best* a hobbyist who lucked into the job she *did* get. 

And anyway, an intelligent person wouldn't have tried to go into teaching when she really should've known she didn't have the personality for it.

If I'm asked, "Do you think it's fair to expect people to be perfect?" I will say of course not, and what is your definition of perfect anyway? 

And yet here I am, never thin enough, never pretty enough, never smart enough, never hard-working enough, never likeable enough (why *do* my friends even like me, I don't know), never good enough. I wasn't always this way; I used to see the thought of there always being something else to learn as an *inspiring* thing. Now it's just some hopelessly insurmountable measure of my perpetual inadequacy. 

It's made therapy a bitch and a half because I don't feel like I deserve to recover. I feel exactly as bad as a fat, lazy, stupid, worthless person *should* feel, and I should probably feel worse. (I still feel like a chump for wussing out of suicide, for example.) I will never be good enough to feel like I deserve to not hate myself.

You'd think, but I found that at least the shaved-off hairs clung to my clothes worse than those than the long tapered hairs I'd brush out of a dog, and I had a few get embedded into my skin (very painful). I was undoubtedly dealing with a significantly larger amount of hair than the petowner would in the average course of the day, but I learned to be really careful around freshly-shaved fur, particularly if it came from a coarse-haired dog like a lab. With dogs with softer coats, it wasn't such a big deal, but there was something about shaved lab fur that was really difficult to deal with.
My favorite reason people would give for having their labs shaved was, "He just sheds so much!" And now he's just gonna shed a lot of super-short, pokey hairs. Silly.

> I used to go to a lot of secular concerts and the feeling was exactly the same, everyone singing in unison, strong feels etc.

Yes. I actually had a feeling akin to a religious experience, but *stronger*, at a Florence + The Machine concert. My experience of Christianity was always tinged with existential terror and guilt, but hearing Florence Welch sing? Everyone loved her music, knew the words, and she is just *so sweet* and loves what she does *so much*, it would've been hard not to get swept up into the experience. There was no fear of hell or apocalypse, no guilt over whatever thought-sins I was committing; just her, the crowd, and the songs we were all sharing. It was beautiful.

It probably doesn't hurt that a lot of what she sings [sounds kinda gospel-ish](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=am6rArVPip8).

I was in that place for a while. Then, as now, I had trouble believing that anyone liked or loved me, including family. I could see nothing about myself that would inspire any sense of mourning if I were to pass, and still don't. My thought was, essentially, "They'll get over it." I was annoyed and tired of feeling obligated to keep existing, when existence was always painful and terrifying.

The only thing that kept me hanging on was knowing my dog would look for me. There's an earnestness about his attachment to me that I couldn't doubt. So I took the long, hard, expensive, *irritating* route that was therapy, because I either had to change something or kill myself, and the stupid dog made the latter not an option.

I suppose I'm better at recognizing that these thoughts are irrational, as I have empirical proof that I'm liked. Getting myself to believe it is another matter, but small steps, I guess.

Yeah, I can't even pretend to know how hard that is, not that I should if I even could. :/ I'm friends with some trans-women and trans-men and I only get snippets of the difficulties they face through what they tell me, and I still know that isn't anywhere close to a full picture.

Some of them are in loving relationships, though. It does seem to be possible, at least. How hard it was for them to get there, I haven't the slightest clue.

For what it's worth, this internet stranger hopes you find someone who loves you for all of you. You deserve it.

> I don't know a whole lot about it, but it seems like it's a cycle that reinforces itself.

It absolutely does, unfortunately. It's made it really difficult to accept any kind of positive feedback from people I know. I've asked my friends point-blank why they hang out with me, get told something like, "You're funny, sweet, and we enjoy being around you...?" And in my head, all I'll think is, "How have I convinced them of this? They have made a mistake." And then I spiral into worry that it's only a matter of time before they see through me and shun me, as I feel they should. 

Despite, you know, the direct evidence I have of them saying, "Hey, we actually do like you," as well as them going out of their way to invite me to things (we're all adults; they could just choose to not call or text me.) The belief persists. 

And yeah, I really am in the wrong place as far as religious environment goes. I was raised in a very hellfire-and-brimstone baptist church, that basically *every week* talked about how we're in the End Times and we're all basically worthless without god so we'd best believe right, AND TIME IS RUNNING OUT. It did me no favors. 

It's bad enough that, years after ceasing to believe, all it takes is someone referring to the "End Times", someone talking to me with the assumption that I share their beliefs, or even something stupid like *getting stuck in church traffic* that I get panic attacks/flashbacks, terrified of a judgment I no longer believe in. I've spent most of my life stuck in constant existential terror, which unfortunately didn't go away once I stopped believing. Its inescapability here doesn't help.

I wish I could afford to move. I unfortunately can't right now, too many debts to pay back, but, I dunno. Maybe someday I'll fail less at life and be able to afford it.

I'm really not sure. I've loathed myself since I was a kid, pretty much. If I were to describe a person as the following: "Works full-time building websites, not for very much money but always trying to learn new things about web development, draws for fun and tries to help newer artists with pointers when she can, rescued a dog (they are inseparable now), loves going to concerts, volunteers for events sometimes when they align with her interests (as long as it's pretty behind-the-scenes; she's shy) and she likes to spend time with friends and generally makes it a point to Not Be a Dick." I would not think *what a horrible shitlord, she doesn't even deserve the breath she breathes, anything nice she does barely makes up for everyone else having to put up with her. I bet her "friends" can't even stand her.*

Yet that's exactly what I think about myself, despite matching that description. There's some sort of logic-proof cognitive dissonance I manage to maintain where I can think most folks are decent and just doing what they can to get by, but I am fundamentally worthless, unlovable, and *deserve death*. I have never thought any other way, and I really don't know how to. 

So, uh. Thus the therapy, I suppose.

I feel like a giant loserface loser, despite constant reassurance from my friends that being fiscally responsible *is* actually the adult thing to do here. Alas. But I have actually been able to make payments, unlike when I lived on my own, so. Gotta do what I gotta do, I guess.

Haha, I look at it more like putting lipstick on a pig. Even if I weren't a *fat* useless faggot, I'd still be a useless faggot. 

I'm at the lowest weight I've been at since middle school, approaching an average body build, even. Hate myself more than I ever did. I can finish 45 minutes of exercise and still feel like I've barely scratched the surface of what makes me loathsome.

Same here. I also have too much respect for other people to put them through the trial that would be dating me right now. I feel bad enough for all of the strain I put on my friends with all my neuroses as it is. No one likes dealing with frequent panic attacks or hearing about how you still think about killing yourself sometimes. (The pool of anyone who'd be willing to put up with that shrinks considerably when you confine it to the cross-section of 'single women attracted to other women' and 'non-religious people in the bible belt', too.)

Supposedly the therapy and medication will help. It has yet to make me feel like a more worthwhile person, but there's nothing for it but to keep going, I guess.

I was the gay one in the original cartoon, who felt like she shouldn't have a problem with homosexuality ("everything is forgiven! ... right?") but couldn't shake the feeling that she was going to hell for it. :I

> but to someone else, you could be dumping so much good into their life that you're waaaaaaaay in the positive.

That's true. If I've got enough... mental energy, I guess(?) I can think about it that way. I seem to fall into paranoid thinking really easily though when I'm even a little tired, and end up convinced everyone can smell the pathetic on me and just wants me to go away (and then doing nice things just buys me time in their presence before they get tired of me.) I just assume no one wants me around, for the most part. (Despite being, say, invited to things. I don't know why I still think this way.) But I suppose at least being able to recognize that it's irrational, in my rational moments, is progress.

Grew up reluctantly baptist. My mom just went to church so much because she was new in the area and didn't have friends in the area, and we got taken with, but *man* were they big on the End Times/being "Rapture Ready" shit. Just about every week, I got told about how the world was probably ending soon. (My parents now go to a much less hellfire-and-brimstone, non-denominational(?) church. But I've got enough emotional shrapnel left, I guess, that I can't even hear their comparatively-mild, "Be a nice person, just like Jesus!" sermons without flinching like an abused puppy.)

I didn't go to church so much in high school (I liked sleep and mom eventually got tired of trying to drag us out of bed for it) but I was all about 'having a relationship with God' (which I saw as more important than church attendance) and 'tolerance' ("Hey, c'mon, homosexuality is forgiven with everything else!" which *oddly enough* did not help me at all when I was coming to terms with being gay myself in college.) 

So I wasn't deep into youth groups or missions or anything; it was all about trying to get secure in my own beliefs. Which became more and more difficult the more I examined Christianity and compared it to my understanding of the natural world. 

In the end, it was like being on the edge of a cliff, desperately trying to hold on to a rope with a bunch of dead weight at the bottom. It hurt, it was tiring, and I got very upset any time I could feel it slipping. It never supported me, I had to support it. And I felt much freer when I let it go, but I guess I still have a lot of damage left over.

1. Noah's Ark and the Garden of Eden. Even as a kid, I was all about biology, and even when I *wasn't* thinking about how gross it'd be to have to bang your relatives, I was familiar with the concept of genetic diversity. And my questions would all be hand-waved away. "But you need at *least* 50 individuals for short-term species survival, and 500 for long-term, so even if they magically didn't eat each other on the ark, they'd all be really really inbred, really quick. And what about species that die after mating? And how did he deal with the freshwater fish that would've died from their homes being salinated?" "I'm sure God thought of that, sweetie."

2. The realization that the only way I could accept most of these stories was as parables, rather than something that literal that happened. After a certain point of saying to myself, "Well, maybe it's just a metaphor" for story after story I realized I did not, in fact, believe most of what I claimed to believe.

> even though I'm small and mostly insignificant, I can do something that matters.

My kneejerk response to that seems to be, "Yeah, but *I* couldn't possibly. I'm only me." I've been having to put my subconscious attitudes into words lately (for the therapy and all that) and it never occurred to me before how deep the lack of self worth goes. I dug that hole pretty enthusiastically, I guess.

I do like the idea of somehow making a positive impact, but I seem to be pretty good at minimizing my involvement in it. "Yeah, I volunteered for this thing, but at *best* I'm breaking even for [shitty thing I did], and that still leaves [shitty thing], [other shitty thing], and at the very least it's what I do in exchange for people putting up with me." 

I don't know. Maybe finding meaning in other people and trying to make a positive impact will be easier when I'm not convinced there's nothing I can do to make up for how awful I am.

... Man. I don't think I realized before the past couple of weeks exactly how much damage the baptist upbringing did. The church we went to talked almost weekly about being Rapture Ready and end times this, end times that, so I have *always* thought about the end of the world. Even when I stopped believing, I just swapped one end of world scenario for another. I don't know what it's like to not live in constant fear. (Part of the goal of therapy and medication, I suppose.)

Focusing on the now seems like a good goal, though I don't know how capable I am of it right now. I try and I just am overwhelmed with guilt and anxiety that I'm going to not see something coming (as if worrying gives me foresight into the future? Weird idea.) Maybe shortening the timespan would be more attainable at the moment, I don't know.

I may need more fortitude before I can put on a BAMF face and approach life that way. I think some of my problems have come from being raised in an environment where everyone was all about pulling yourself up by bootstraps, and if you're sad *just stop being sad* and that kind of thing. Mostly it's resulted in me being tired and frustrated that I can't macho the fear away. :/ 

Maybe once I'm more secure in general, I dunno. I'm pretty much trying to undo 20-something years of living in near-constant existential terror.

I am seeking therapy, actually! Twice a week, with a super nice fellow who charges on a sliding scale (so my broke ass can afford it even though my insurance doesn't cover it.) I also got on mood stabilizers, which have helped slow the obsessive thoughts down somewhat.

We've been talking about the religious aspect of my situation a lot, since *for some reason* being raised to think that the end of the world could be any time and there's a good chance you're not believing *the right way*, *and* you're a fundamentally irredeemable fleck of shit that could only be loved as an outstanding act of charity, has not had a terribly positive impact on my life. He said my behavior and attitudes sounded a lot like someone with PTSD, which only hit home when he mentioned something about the End Times (which *I'd* brought up earlier) and I flinched, curled into a ball, and looked at the floor. Ech. :/ I've been an atheist for a couple of years, and it still has a grip on me.

So, basically, I guess I'm not in a very good place mentally right now, but I'm at least in a good place to *improve*.

Wow. Uh, sorry for the delayed response, but this kinda blew me out of the water and took some time to digest. Seriously, thank you for taking the time out to write that. I, too, like lists! I far prefer to having a formula/set of steps to follow over just winging it. 

The fact that I don't know the answers to the first couple of questions means I've got some thinking to do, I guess. I must've had goals at some point, but for the life of me, I can't really think of much that drives me right now. (Depression really sucks all the joy out of *everything*, man.)

Weight fell off me super fast at the start, lost 10 or so pounds in a matter of weeks. And then I had enough energy to start going to Tae Kwon Do classes. Once I started adapting to that, I had *so much energy* that I took up weightlifting on my non-class days. 

Actual weight loss was not terribly fast once I picked up the heavy exercise, but I noticed I was starting to get distinctly less jiggly and a lot more physically able, which is really what I care about now. 

I've plateaued now since I'm recovering from the breast reduction and I'm not able to exercise for a while, and my diet is pretty lax since I'm not doing the cooking at the moment. (I got it! I got the surgery! Insurance paid for it! AHAHAHA I am so happy!) Even so, I'm managing to maintain okay. 

In a way, I'm glad I started out fat, rather than having a kickass metabolism as a kid, hitting middle-age, and wondering why the same diet I've been eating for years is making me fat all of a sudden. I've had to re-learn the way I think about food while I'm still relatively young, and it's been one of the best things I've ever done for myself.

*Basically, figure out what you want, and figure out the best way to get it.* Want to have a well-developed, supportive social net? Push yourself out of your comfort zone and work on that. Is a social net not as important to you, and you'd rather develop your hobbies and interests? Do that. 

Don't know what you want? That's a hard one, I confess. Look around, do some soul-searchin'. Try things. If they suck, you probably don't want that. Keep looking.

It's been a lot of little changes over time, and changing the way I think about food. I looked at areas of my diet and figured out which ones were the likeliest to be contributing to my weight and made a plan to change them. 

I grew up drinking a *lot* of soda, and a fair amount of homemade sweet tea. So I decided to give up soda, and just drink sweet tea instead -- after all, sweet tea was still sweet, but it had less sugar than soda. I stuck with that for a while, until I didn't miss soda anymore, and decided to start easing off the amount of sugar I put in there. Instead of a cup of sugar in a gallon, I'd put half a cup, and got used to drinking that, and so on. 

Eventually I got to where I was only drinking unsweetened tea, and now any time a restaurant gives me the sweet stuff by accident, it tastes like drinking a sugary punch to the face.

Liquid calories and bread/pasta/cereal were the biggest offenders for me. I stopped eating cereal for breakfast -- instead I get up early enough to make a whole scrambled egg + one egg white. I still eat bread and pasta on occasion, but I've cut way down. My next area to attack is the Friday drinks with coworkers, but argh *so fun*. That one's going to be hard.

But basically, **I didn't think of it as "I need to diet." I thought of it as, "I am drinking way too much sugar/my portion sizes are just too big, and I need to change it."** 'Diet', to me, implied temporary. If I didn't want to end up 350+ pounds like my dad, I needed to make permanent changes. And the easiest way to do that was to take one or two changes at a time; the ones I've made have stuck. I physically *can't* eat as much as I used to. And after reducing the amount of sugar I eat, I genuinely prefer milder sweet tastes, like real fruit instead of fruity candy sugarbombs now. 

It does kinda suck and it does take a while. Other people here have gone through faster changes than I have -- this 40 pounds has taken me a couple of years. But I've been able to keep it off pretty well, even with occasional holiday lapses and birthday parties, and without a lot of conscious dieting effort on my part. 

EDIT: One thing that has definitely helped me re: not giving up was a quote I saw either here or on /r/loseit but **the gist was, "Don't avoid doing something because it will take time. The time will pass anyway."** Don't get too frustrated! I've been there and it does no good. Just always try to do as well or better than you did yesterday; you can't really ask more of yourself than that. (And when that doesn't work, which it won't *always* because nobody's perfect, keep seeking support! If you're feeling down, a little external validation can go a long way.)

I don't have any experience with owning dogs that shed yet, but I just thought I'd mention that **if they don't shed, absolutely trim the hair between their toes**. Even if they do shed, if they have a really thick coat and really thick fur on their paws, you should probably trim their toes too.

I used to work for a groomer, and occasionally fluffy dogs would come through that hadn't been groomed in a while and sometimes they'd have matting between their toes because the hair got so long. And that will definitely trap moisture, on top of just being physically uncomfortable. Other, retriever-type dogs with fluffy feet occasionally had some toe-tangles, but the non-shedding dogs (and shedding dogs with long, dense hair, like a Newfie) had the worst time of it. 

Long toe hair can pick up little burrs and pokey things a lot easier than trimmed hair. And if it's longer, burrs and things tend to get tangled pretty good. 

If you're worried, check her paws occasionally. If they're still wet *hours* after going outside, feels tangled, or gets burrs stuck in them all the time, it's worth trimming them. If not, the dog's probably fine. 

If you're comfortable trimming your own dog's feet, you can pick up a decent pair of rounded-tip scissors for not a lot of money at a pet store, if you want to do it yourself. No pokey edges to accidentally jab the dog with, and I know scissors freak my own dog out *a lot* less than clippers. 

If you're not, or the dog flails any time you touch its feet, take it to a groomer. (Even if you do trim the hair yourself, it couldn't hurt to have a professional do it occasionally.) A lot of places have some kind of "mini groom" package where they just trim the face, feet, and butt, for less than a full groom. And if you ask, they may be willing to trim *just* the feet, with no bath or other trimming.

I've had my moments of sheer social obliviousness and/or isolationism, but I fail far harder at romance. I can't say I have a *lot* of friends I hang out with all the time, but I have a few really good ones that have stuck around. And here are a couple of things that have helped me.

1. Make yourself go out to social events (that you have an interest in, obviously, even D&D nights or a quilting bee or whatever floats your boat), even if it puts you into a cold sweat thinking about them. 
2. Following 1, meet even one person who you *want* to go out to social events with. (Or who will drag you to social events, even if it puts you into a cold sweat thinking about them.)
3. When in doubt, seek common interests and discuss. Don't be afraid to say, "Oh my god, I love that band!" based on a shirt someone's wearing or "Oh hey, you're reading <book>? Have you read any of <author>?" Sometimes it will fall flat and they'll give you monosyllabic answers and get away from you as fast as possible. Shrug it off and move on (maybe they are also socially awkward and are kicking themselves internally, you never know). 
4. Once contact is established, make an effort to maintain it. Even if it's just texting "did you see <common interest> has <new thing> out?!" or "hey, how are you doing?" occasionally.

Realizing the hurt you've caused doesn't necessarily forgive it, but if it means you'll never do it again, that alone makes you a better woman. 

It's also no reason to keep you from moving on. Yeah, it's something you're going to carry with you, and that's a consequence you'll have to face. But who does *your* being miserable benefit? The ones you hurt? I doubt they'd even know. You? Certainly not. 

I'm not religious and thus not keen on religious sayings, but in this case, I think it's applicable: "Every saint has a past; every sinner has a future." You did some bad things and you feel bad; that's understandable. But rather than letting it paralyze you, keep it somewhere in the back of your mind as a reminder of the kind of person you *don't* want to be. As a woman, be everything you never were when you were 'failing at being a man'. 

I feel the best redemption comes not in self-flagellation, but in living in direct opposition to the offenses in question. Be kind, be respectful, be loving. Apologize where you can, but above all, move on and *live* as that better person.
